value.overview: The Streak-headed Woodcreeper is a slender, medium-sized tree-climbing bird of the ovenbird family. It has a long, slightly curved bill, strongly streaked head and breast, olive-brown upperparts, and a reddish-brown rump and tail. It is widespread from Mexico through Central America into northern South America. In Costa Rica, it is one of the most widespread and regularly encountered woodcreepers of lowland and foothill habitats.
value.classification: The Streak-headed Woodcreeper belongs to the family Furnariidae and subfamily Dendrocolaptinae, the woodcreepers. Its scientific name is Lepidocolaptes souleyetii.
value.identification: This woodcreeper is about 19 cm long. Adults show bold pale buff and dark streaks on the crown, sides of the head, neck, upper back, and breast. The back is olive-brown, while the rump, wings, and tail are warm rufous or cinnamon-brown. The bill is fairly long, slender, and slightly decurved, often with a pale or pinkish lower mandible. It is distinguished from the similar Spot-crowned Woodcreeper by streaks, rather than spots, on the crown.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Mexico through Central America to northern South America, including Colombia, Venezuela, and Ecuador. In Costa Rica it is a resident on the lowlands of both the Caribbean and Pacific slopes, locally reaching about 1,500 meters. It is most common in humid regions and becomes less frequent west of the Central Valley and in the dry northwest. It uses forest canopy and edges, older second growth, gallery forest, tree plantations, mangroves, and other habitats retaining mature trees.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and generally non-migratory across its range. It remains present year-round on both Costa Rican slopes, although local movements may occur in response to food or breeding conditions.
value.breeding: The nest is placed in a narrow cavity or crevice in a living or dead tree, and may occasionally occupy an abandoned woodpecker hole. It is lined with pieces of bark or other coarse material. In Costa Rica, nests have been recorded approximately 4.5 to 24 meters above the ground. A typical clutch contains two eggs. Incubation lasts about 15 days, and nestlings remain in the nest for roughly 19 days.
value.dietFeeding: The Streak-headed Woodcreeper feeds mainly on arthropods, including insects and spiders. It searches bark, crevices, lichens, and epiphytes while climbing trunks and larger branches, using its slender bill to probe for prey. It usually forages from the understory to the middle or upper canopy, especially along forest edges and in semi-open woodland. Its ability to use second growth and plantations helps it persist in modified landscapes with suitable trees.
value.behavior: It usually forages alone or in pairs and may occasionally occur in small groups of about three birds. Unlike many woodcreepers, it is not commonly associated with mixed-species feeding flocks. It climbs upward along trunks and branches, bracing its stiff tail against the bark. Its call and song include thin, high-pitched notes and a characteristic sputtering or descending trill. It is active in the canopy and at forest edges, but can approach gardens and houses where trees remain.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is not considered to be declining at a rate that qualifies the species for a threatened category.
